The First 100 Days End With a Judge in Handcuffs and a Country in Contested Terrain

As the administration marked its symbolic milestone, courts, universities, and the press each became fresh battlegrounds

```markdown The week that closed out the first hundred days of Donald Trump's second term did not offer the traditional rituals of a presidential milestone. Instead it delivered a sitting judge in handcuffs, a permanent court order against a wartime deportation law, a Supreme Court justice's public rebuke of her own government, and a Cabinet meeting held against the backdrop of a shrinking economy. Across seven days, courts, universities, and news organizations each became sites of new pressure from the executive branch, while the judiciary pushed back with a force that was neither uniform nor guaranteed to last.

The weekend set the tone. FBI agents arrested Milwaukee County Circuit Judge Hannah Dugan on obstruction charges, accusing her of helping a man evade immigration agents inside her own courthouse. The FBI director publicized the arrest with a handcuffed photograph, an unusual move for a sitting judicial officer, and the image circulated widely within hours. That same weekend, Trump took to Truth Social to argue that due process was impractical for the "millions and millions" of people he said the government intended to deport, insisting that officials already knew who among them was a criminal. An arrest inside a courtroom and a public argument against courtroom process itself arrived together — and would recur throughout the week.

Universities absorbed a parallel wave of pressure. The administration continued threatening federal funding for schools, including Swarthmore, over claims they had failed to address antisemitic harassment, while Columbia, Harvard, and other institutions moved to discipline students involved in pro-Palestinian protests. Critics said the discipline fell disproportionately on Palestinian, Arab, Muslim, and other minority students. This became one of two distinct storylines involving federal leverage over civil society: one running through campuses and protest discipline, the other, emerging days later, through the Justice Department's own civil rights enforcement staff.

Press freedom eroded on several fronts at once. The Associated Press was barred from the Oval Office and the presidential pool. The Department of Justice, under Attorney General Pam Bondi, rescinded a policy that had shielded journalists from being compelled to reveal confidential sources. Trump separately singled out a New York Times reporter by name, calling her "biased and untalented," while legal pressure built against ABC, CBS, and the Des Moines Register. Funding threats against NPR and PBS were already in motion — a thread that would culminate later in the week with an executive order.

Congress, meanwhile, advanced a budget framework enabling large tax cuts alongside proposed reductions to Medicaid and SNAP, plus $68.8 billion in new border security spending. Republican divisions over savings targets surfaced almost immediately. And in one of the week's most disturbing enforcement stories, ICE deportations swept up U.S. citizen children along with their immigrant mothers — including a four-year-old with cancer sent abroad without her medication — with little chance for legal intervention beforehand.

By Monday, the administration had moved from rhetoric to formal executive action. Trump signed a cluster of orders requiring English proficiency for commercial drivers, directing agencies to identify and defund "sanctuary jurisdictions," and expanding legal protections for police officers, including a review of consent decrees that had constrained local law enforcement. The same day, reporting revealed a new private club in Georgetown, backed by Donald Trump Jr. and megadonor Omeed Malik, charging more than half a million dollars for membership and direct access to administration officials — already reportedly carrying a waiting list. Separately, the administration quietly ended federal investigations and lawsuits against 89 corporations, a number of which had donated heavily to Trump's inaugural fund.

Not every institutional signal Monday favored the executive branch. A federal appeals court restored an injunction blocking the administration's attempt to fire 90 percent of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's staff, and another judge ordered the restoration of congressionally appropriated funds to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty — a reminder that the executive cannot unilaterally withhold money Congress has already approved. But the day's other major development cut the opposite way: Trump's DOJ appointees removed senior civil servants overseeing the department's voting rights section and directed attorneys to drop active cases, the start of a hollowing-out that would leave the Civil Rights Division a fraction of its former size within days. That evening, Hakeem Jeffries and Cory Booker led a twelve-hour sit-in on the Capitol steps opposing the proposed cuts to Medicaid and SNAP, while Bishop William J. Barber II was arrested during a related demonstration.

Tuesday's developments were quieter in volume but no less consequential. Human Rights Watch described the detention of Venezuelan migrant Neiyerver Rengel and at least 252 others as "enforced disappearances," after families lost track of relatives deported to El Salvador on gang-affiliation accusations. House Republicans added a procedural rule blocking a vote on investigating Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's use of Signal for sensitive communications, narrowing Congress's ability to examine a potential security lapse. The Peace Corps began a second round of deferred resignations tied to a DOGE review, and Hegseth formally ended the Pentagon's Women, Peace and Security program, which had originated in Trump's first term. Nearly 400 scientific contributors to the National Climate Assessment were dismissed the same day a federal appeals court upheld an injunction blocking DOGE from accessing sensitive Social Security data — one action reducing scientific capacity, the other preserving a check on executive reach into personal records. By day's end, the Federal Election Commission lost its quorum after a second commissioner resigned, leaving the country's campaign finance watchdog unable to act.

Wednesday arrived as the symbolic marker of the administration's first hundred days, and the day split cleanly between image and consequence. Trump held a Cabinet meeting celebrating the milestone, during which Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. repeated debunked claims about child trafficking under the previous administration, while Trump responded to a newly reported GDP contraction by blaming his predecessor. Away from the cameras, the legal ground was shifting. U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. — a Trump appointee — ruled that the administration's invocation of the 1798 Alien Enemies Act "exceeds the scope" of the statute and permanently enjoined its use against a certified class of Venezuelan migrants in the Southern District of Texas. The same day, the Supreme Court issued an emergency order blocking the deportation of Javier Salazar, a 19-year-old Venezuelan migrant with no criminal record, preserving his chance to contest removal. A separate federal judge ordered the release of Palestinian Columbia student Mohsen Mahdawi from ICE detention, ruling that his continued confinement would likely chill protected speech and comparing the administration's approach to McCarthyism. At a Michigan rally that evening, Trump attacked "communist radical-left judges" and called on the Supreme Court to intervene on his behalf — rhetoric that extended directly from the weekend's arrest of Judge Dugan. Beneath all of it, the economic numbers were real: the Bureau of Economic Analysis reported the first GDP contraction in three years, and weekly unemployment claims rose to their highest level since February, both linked in part to tariff disruption.

Thursday deepened both the press-freedom and economic threads. Trump signed an executive order directing the Corporation for Public Broadcasting to end funding for NPR and PBS, accusing the outlets of biased coverage; PBS President Paula Kerger called the move "blatantly unlawful," and both organizations signaled they would challenge it in court. The order followed directly from the weekend's press restrictions and the DOJ's rollback of source protections, forming a single continuous story about the administration's effort to reshape the country's information environment rather than a series of disconnected incidents. The same day, Trump signed an order creating a Religious Liberty Commission, naming Dr. Phil McGraw among its members. On the economic front, UPS confirmed plans to lay off 20,000 employees and close 73 facilities, while port executives in Los Angeles and Oakland projected shipping volumes could fall more than 35 percent because of tariffs — concrete, verifiable consequences following directly from the contraction reported a day earlier. Congress declined to check the president's tariff authority: House Republicans used a procedural rule to block a Democratic effort to challenge the national emergency tariff declaration, and Senate Republicans voted down a related measure. Reporting also confirmed that the Civil Rights Division had lost 70 percent of its attorneys since January — more than 250 departures or reassignments — a stark measure of the institutional hollowing that had begun on Monday. And in a moment that captured the week's central tension, Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson publicly condemned the administration's rhetoric toward judges as deliberate intimidation undermining the rule of law, a direct rebuke that traced back to the president's Michigan rally remarks and, further still, to the arrest of Judge Dugan five days earlier. Oklahoma's new social studies standards, meanwhile, drew criticism for requiring students to analyze supposed 2020 election discrepancies and for sharply increasing religious content in public school curriculum.

The week closed with two of its major throughlines reaching a form of resolution, both contested. Judge Rodriguez certified a class of Venezuelan detainees and issued his permanent injunction against use of the Alien Enemies Act, cementing the judicial limit first announced Wednesday. And Trump announced on Truth Social that his administration would revoke Harvard University's tax-exempt status, escalating a monthslong standoff over funding and diversity policy — a threat that remained unresolved and contested rather than a settled outcome. Swarthmore issued interim suspensions without full due process to nine students involved in a protest encampment, extending the week's pattern of campus discipline. The Justice Department paused Foreign Corrupt Practices Act prosecutions for six months and abruptly closed its cryptocurrency crime unit following criticism from industry donors, echoing Monday's decision to drop investigations into 89 corporate donors. In Oklahoma City, ICE agents posing as U.S. Marshals raided the wrong home, taking a citizen family's belongings despite the family not being the intended target. Former pardon attorney Liz Oyer said Trump's recent pardons of white-collar offenders had erased more than $1 billion in restitution and penalties owed by wealthy Americans. And in a smaller but telling coda, Maine's federal child-nutrition funds were restored after the state sued over a funding freeze tied to its refusal to bar transgender athletes from girls' sports — a reminder that even contested federal leverage over states still had to answer, eventually, to legal process.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a government testing the outer edges of executive power on several fronts simultaneously — over courts, campuses, the press, immigration enforcement, and the machinery of civil rights enforcement itself — while the judiciary, unevenly but repeatedly, pushed back. A judge was arrested and handcuffed; another judge, appointed by the same president, ruled his invocation of an 18th-century wartime statute unlawful. A justice of the Supreme Court warned publicly that attacks on the judiciary amounted to intimidation, even as the president continued making them. Public broadcasters faced defunding while a private club sold access to Cabinet officials for half a million dollars a seat, and pardons erased more than a billion dollars in penalties owed by the well-connected even as ordinary families lost their possessions to a mistaken immigration raid. None of these threads resolved neatly by Friday. Litigation over Harvard's tax status, the fate of NPR and PBS funding, and the broader reach of the Alien Enemies Act ruling all remained open. What the week made clear was less a verdict than a pattern: the steady, simultaneous testing of institutional limits across courts, universities, the press, and federal agencies, met by a judiciary that in several instances held the line — and in several others did not yet have the chance to. ```
